meta.operativeContentRazor: NOTHING in this file is a procedure a reader could run. Where a criticism work describes an operative rite (White on alchemical and sexual rites, Bharati on mantra and nyāsa, Brooks on Śrīvidyā pūjā, Eliade on prāṇāyāma), the row records THAT the scholar describes it, at what level of detail, and with `sourceLayer: secondary-scholarship` so the completeness grade is never mistaken for a grade of a primary text. No mantra syllable, quantity, timing, substance, sequence or second-person instruction appears anywhere here. Per this round's standing order, no quoted operative text ships: the FRAMING §10 blockers (B1-B4) gate the first quotation and are not cleared.
meta.livingPeopleAndLiveDisputes: Kripal, Doniger, Malhotra, Nicholson, Young, Urban, White, Singleton, Mallinson, Wedemeyer, Tyagananda, Vrajaprana, Caldwell, Sanderson and Brooks are living or recently active; the Ramakrishna Math and Mission, the Sivananda/ISYVC organisation, Siddha Yoga/SYDA, the Osho movement, the TM organisation and the Infinity Foundation are organised communities with active stakes. EVERY contested row here carries every position with the holder named, and NONE is adjudicated. Where an allegation is of criminal or professional misconduct the row states who alleged it, in what venue, on what date, and what the documented outcome was — including 'no formal proceeding' and 'no consensus' as outcomes. Absence of an outcome is recorded as absence, never as vindication or as guilt.

edgeVocabularyExtension.note: This slice needs relation types the earlier slices did not. Declared here rather than smuggled in.

new.REFUTES: X argues Y's central claim is false. Always a CLAIM, never a verdict; requires `basis` naming the kind of evidence offered.
new.REFRAMES: X accepts Y's data but argues the category or framing is the artefact — e.g. 'tantra' as a colonial-scholarly construct.
new.CRITICISES_TRANSLATION: X alleges specific renderings in Y are wrong. `basis` must name at least one disputed term or the claim is not admissible.
new.ALLEGES_MISATTRIBUTION: X argues Y's stated author/authorship is wrong or incomplete.
new.REDATES: X argues Y (or a practice Y describes) belongs to a different period.
new.DEFENDS: X answers a criticism of Y on the merits.
new.RESPONDS_TO: X is a formal reply to X's critic; weaker than DEFENDS, does not imply success.
new.ALLEGES_PLAGIARISM: X alleges textual appropriation by Y. Requires venue, date, and documented outcome.
new.LEGAL_ACTION_AGAINST: A filed proceeding or formal complaint against a work. Requires forum, statute, date, disposition.
new.SUPERSEDED_BY_COLLABORATION: Two works once read as opposed whose authors later co-published — recorded because it is the cleanest evidence that a 'dispute' was partly manufactured by readers.

completenessVocabulary.n/a-secondary: The work contains no procedure of its own. Used for pure criticism and polemic. It is NOT a defect grade.
completenessVocabulary.sourceLayerNote: Any procedure row on a criticism work carries `sourceLayer: 'secondary-scholarship'`. Its completeness grade describes the SCHOLAR'S DESCRIPTION, never the underlying rite.

works.title: The Tantric Tradition
works.author: Agehananda Bharati (b. Leopold Fischer, Vienna 1923 – Pittsford NY 1991); ordained a Daśanāmī saṃnyāsin; Professor of Anthropology, Syracuse University
works.culture: Euro-American academic anthropology of religion, written from inside the Hindu monastic order
works.dateText: first published London: Rider, 1965 (so the Internet Archive scan and this round's brief) or 1966 (so the Wikipedia article), revised 1975

editions.publisher: Rider & Co., London
Rider (revised edition); later Samuel Weiser / Grove reprints

works.whatIsCriticised: A WHOLE FRAMING, plus specific translations. Bharati's target is the Western occult-revival literature on tantra — the theosophical and popular-esoteric writing that treated tantra as a secret sexual-spiritual technology — and the Orientalist editions that fed it. He writes as an initiate holding the material to a philological and anthropological standard the popularisers never met.
works.evidenceOffered: Initiatory access plus Sanskrit competence plus fieldwork; his standing claim is that he is judging the literature against the tradition as it is actually transmitted, not against a reconstructed ideal. THE BOOK ITSELF WAS NOT READ THIS ROUND; the characterisation above is from catalogue and encyclopedia description (C2, C3) and is the weakest link in this row.
works.whoDisputes: Not established this round. No published rebuttal to The Tantric Tradition was located, which is itself a finding worth recording rather than a licence to treat the book as unopposed.
works.currentState: The book is still routinely cited as the first serious study of the field by an initiate. Its polemical half — that most previous authors abused the subject — is treated in the later literature (Urban, C6) as an early instance of the constructivist critique rather than as its final word.

procedures.evidence: The book is described in catalogue and reference sources as a systematic study of Hindu and Buddhist tantric mantra and sādhana. Whether it reproduces operative sequences at usable detail was NOT checked. Recorded as 'referenced' pending a read; an auditor should treat this grade as unverified.

works.title: 'The Hindu Renaissance and its Apologetic Patterns' — the paper that coins the PIZZA EFFECT
works.author: Agehananda Bharati
works.culture: Euro-American academic anthropology of religion

editions.publisher: The Journal of Asian Studies 29.2 (Association for Asian Studies), pp. 267-287

works.whatIsCriticised: A WHOLE FRAMING — the authenticity claim itself. Bharati names the mechanism by which a practice is simplified or elaborated abroad and then re-imported to its homeland with enhanced prestige, so that the 'traditional' form now defended at home is in part a foreign reconstruction. He illustrates it with pizza (a plain Southern Italian peasant bread elaborated in America and returned to Italy) and applies it to Indian religion.
works.evidenceOffered: A set of named cases rather than a statistical argument: the Maharishi Mahesh Yogi's movement and ISKCON gaining Indian standing after Western success; postural yoga and its gurus; the Bhagavad Gītā's elevation to something like a Hindu Bible under Western pressure to find one; and Satyajit Ray's Apu films, praised abroad before being reappraised at home.
works.whoDisputes: Extended rather than refuted. Stephen Jenkins notes the loop can iterate (American pizza tourists seeking 'authentic' Italian pizza, prompting Italian responses that then shape American authenticity ideas). Jørn Borup proposes an 'inverted pizza effect' for European philosophers — Heidegger is his case — inspired by Eastern thought already filtered through Western readings, which then feeds back to Eastern thinkers. Mark Sedgwick applies it outside religion to reinterpreted martyrdom in Islamist terrorism.
works.currentState: The term is standard vocabulary in the study of modern Hinduism and modern yoga. It is DIRECTLY LOAD-BEARING for this survey: any claim that a repo-listed Eastern practice is 'the traditional form' has to survive a pizza-effect test, because the version reaching the compiler may be the re-imported one.
works.proceduresNote: n/a-secondary — a journal article of analysis; contains no procedure.
works.dedupWith: No repo record of the concept. The repo has the RAW MATERIAL for it — the Krishnamacharya/Mysore-palace record and the Pierre Bernard record both describe re-export loops — but never names the mechanism.
works.siteRelevance: HIGHEST in this slice. Proposed as a framing note attached to every modern-guru and modern-yoga record in the atlas.

works.title: Sir John Woodroffe, Tantra and Bengal: 'An Indian Soul in a European Body?'
works.author: Kathleen Taylor
works.culture: British academic Indology / history of Orientalism (SOAS Studies on South Asia)
works.dateText: 2001 (Curzon); reissued Routledge 2014; based on doctoral work of the 1990s

editions.publisher: Curzon Press, Richmond (ISBN 070071345X)
Routledge (ISBN 9780415749367)

works.whatIsCriticised: AN ATTRIBUTION. The single most consequential authorship claim in the Western tantra corpus: that 'Arthur Avalon' — the name on the Tantrik Texts series, the Mahānirvāṇa translation, Shakti and Shakta and The Serpent Power — was not one Englishman but a collaboration, and that the Sanskrit competence behind it was substantially that of the Bengali scholar Atal Bihari Ghose (1864-1936).
works.evidenceOffered: DOCUMENTARY AND SELF-INCRIMINATING, which is what makes this row unusually strong. Taylor points to Woodroffe's own prefaces, where he states that he published under the Avalon name to signal that the works were written with the direct cooperation of others and that he did not desire sole credit for what was as much their work as his. Taylor then identifies the unnamed chief collaborator as Ghose, and separately assesses Woodroffe's own relationship to Sanskrit, arguing he made very extensive — though skilled — use of secondary sources and of Ghose's and other Indians' knowledge.
works.whoDisputes: No sustained rebuttal located. The claim is now the received account and the repo already carries it as one of two positions on the Avalon record.
works.currentState: Settled enough to be the default in reference works, but the repo's two-position treatment is the right register and should stay: 'Woodroffe as sole author-translator' is a position with a real historical constituency (it is how the books were read for eighty years), not a straw man.
works.proceduresNote: n/a-secondary — a biography and authorship study.

works.title: Tantra: Sex, Secrecy, Politics, and Power in the Study of Religion
works.author: Hugh B. Urban (Ohio State University, Department of Comparative Studies)
works.culture: American academic history of religions; genealogical / constructivist method

editions.publisher: University of California Press, Berkeley & Los Angeles, xvi+372 pp. (ISBN 0520236564)

works.whatIsCriticised: THE CATEGORY ITSELF. Urban's claim is that 'Tantra' as a unified object is not a datum the scholar found but an artefact the scholarly and popular imaginations jointly produced — formed in the interplay between Orientalist scholars, Christian missionaries, colonial administrators, Indian reformers and, later, Western marketers. He argues it functions as a 'dialectical image' reflecting the interests of whoever deploys it.
works.evidenceOffered: Genealogical: the history of the term's use. He documents the Victorian construction in which tantra was cast as the most degenerate example of the 'Indian mind' — a pathological mixture of sensuality and religion held responsible for Hinduism's decline — and traces the mirror-image modern construction in which the same material becomes a liberatory sexual spirituality.
works.whoDisputes: Urban explicitly refuses the simpler postcolonial version of his own argument (Kripal's jacket assessment credits him with declining to narrate 'yet another postcolonial narrative about the evil West'). The standing counter-position in the field is philological rather than polemical: Sanderson's manuscript-based reconstruction (crit:sanderson-saiva-age) treats the Śaiva corpus as a real, datable, internally structured tradition whose existence does not depend on the colonial category. THESE ARE NOT STRICTLY INCOMPATIBLE and this file does not treat them as a contradiction.
works.currentState: The constructivist reading is mainstream for the WORD and its reception history; it is not generally taken to dissolve the Sanskrit corpus. Both halves are needed: the texts are real, the umbrella term is a modern artefact.
works.dedupWith: repo: confluence.js already cites Urban 2003 and Urban's 'The Omnipotent Oom' (Esoterica 3, 2001) on the Pierre Bernard record, and already states there that the tantra-equals-sacred-sexuality equation is a modern construction. THIS SLICE ADDS the book as a node in its own right with its thesis stated, so that other rows can point at it.
works.siteRelevance: Second only to the pizza effect. Any repo page that uses 'tantra' as an umbrella needs this row behind it.

works.whatIsCriticised: A WHOLE FRAMING, aimed in two directions at once. Against the modern Western 'tantric sex' industry, White argues the original South Asian rites were not about mutual ecstasy at all but about the ritual production, exchange and consumption of sexual fluids understood as power-substances. Against the sanitising Indian and scholarly readings, he argues the transgressive material is literal and central rather than symbolic.
works.evidenceOffered: Sanskrit textual work, iconography, translations and ethnographic material — reviewers including Gerald James Larson credit it as densely cited and richly illustrated.
works.whoDisputes: TWO DISTINCT OBJECTIONS, and they should not be merged. (1) EVIDENTIARY: a reviewer's objection recorded in the reception literature runs that White proves the early tantrics MAY WELL have ingested these fluids but cannot prove that they DID, and that he infers non-performance of an alternative only because the alternative could not be done — an inference-to-the-only-available-explanation complaint. (2) COMMUNITY: the Trinidadian Hindu priest Pandita Indrani Rampersad is recorded as accusing White of demolishing tantra. Reception commentary also notes that much of the hostile popular review traffic came from people who had not read the book — recorded as a claim made in that commentary, not as a verified fact about individual reviewers.
works.currentState: Contested and live. Wedemeyer's 2013 book (crit:wedemeyer-making-sense) is the most substantial published challenge to the whole literal-transgression framing that White represents at its strongest.

works.title: 'The Śaiva Age: The Rise and Dominance of Śaivism during the Early Medieval Period'
works.author: Alexis Sanderson (formerly Spalding Professor of Eastern Religions and Ethics, Oxford)
works.culture: British/European philological Indology; manuscript-based reconstruction

editions.publisher: In Shingo Einoo (ed.), Genesis and Development of Tantrism (Tokyo: Institute of Oriental Culture, University of Tokyo), Institute of Oriental Culture Special Series 23, pp. 41-350

works.whatIsCriticised: A PERIODISATION AND A DIRECTION OF BORROWING. Two claims of very different strength are usually bundled together under this title and this slice separates them. (a) THE PERIODISATION: that Śaivism was the dominant religion of the early medieval Indian polity, sustained by royal patronage — a claim about institutions, argued from epigraphy and manuscript evidence. (b) THE DEPENDENCY: that the Buddhist Yoginītantras drew substantially on the Śaiva Vidyāpīṭha corpus. Sanderson's own formulation is more nuanced than the version that circulates: the relationship is presented as bidirectional, with Śaiva Vidyāpīṭha material shaping the Buddhist Yoginītantras and Buddhist Śākta material later flowing back into the Śāktism of Bengal.
works.evidenceOffered: PHILOLOGICAL AND OF THE STRONGEST AVAILABLE KIND for a transmission claim — shared passages, shared errors, manuscript witnesses, colophons, inscriptions. This is the method the repo's own transmission discipline is modelled on: a dependency edge needs documented textual dependency, not resemblance.
works.whoDisputes: THREE POSITIONS, of very different evidentiary weight. (1) Christian Wedemeyer, Making Sense of Tantric Buddhism (Columbia, 2013), argues against explaining Buddhist tantric transgression by 'slavish imitation of Śaiva traditions' — one of three explanations he treats as fallacious, alongside lusty monks and primitive tribal survivals — while crediting Sanderson's identification of non-dual understanding as a hallmark of Hindu tantra. (2) Ronald Davidson, Indian Esoteric Buddhism (Columbia, 2002), locates both traditions within the feudalisation of early medieval society, with competing tantric lineages drawing on shared indigenous and tribal goddess cults as well as on one another — a shared-substrate account rather than a directional one. (3) A NON-SCHOLARLY counter-current, represented here only by a Substack essay, holds that the whole argument presupposes what it must prove, namely that Śaiva tantras predate Buddhist ones. That source is a blog and is cited as evidence of circulation only.
works.currentState: The periodisation is close to consensus. The dependency direction is genuinely open: the honest statement is that Sanderson's philological case is the strongest single body of evidence on the table and that the shared-substrate alternative has not been refuted by it. THIS FILE DOES NOT PICK.

works.whatIsCriticised: THIS ROW IS THE OBJECT, NOT THE CRITIC. Eliade's yoga book is the twentieth century's most widely read synthesis of the subject and the principal channel by which a comparative, essentialising picture of yoga entered general Western culture. Its edition history is confirmed only in outline here (1933 thesis, French translation about three years later, wide academic impact in Romania and abroad).

works.whoDisputes: THE METHOD, on several distinct grounds, and the fetch this round was thin — see the gap note. The general criticism of Eliade's scholarship recorded in reference sources is threefold: overgeneralisation; lack of empirical support for the broad theoretical frameworks; and the bearing of far-right and nationalist commitments on the work. Two named book-length treatments were located and are given their own rows: Strenski (1987) and Wasserstrom (1999).
works.currentState: Eliade is read historiographically now rather than as a current authority on yoga; the philological corpus (Sanderson, Mallinson, Birch) has replaced him for factual questions while his framing continues to shape popular understanding — itself a pizza-effect-adjacent process.

procedures.evidence: That the book surveys yogic disciplines including breath control is definitional to the work; nothing about its operative detail was checked. NOT a licence to treat Eliade as a procedure source.

works.title: Religion after Religion: Gershom Scholem, Mircea Eliade, and Henry Corbin at Eranos
works.author: Steven M. Wasserstrom
works.culture: American academic history of religions; critique of the history-of-religions school itself

editions.publisher: Princeton University Press (ISBN 9780691005409); JSTOR j.ctt7pds6

works.whatIsCriticised: A SCHOOL AND ITS ETHICS. Wasserstrom argues that Scholem, Eliade and Corbin — all three lecturing to the Eranos circle in Ascona between 1949 and 1978 — jointly overturned the study of religion by de-emphasising law, ritual and social history in favour of myth and mysticism, each locating the symbolism of mystical experience at the centre of his monotheistic tradition. His sharpest charge is ethical rather than philological: that this theory of religion minimised the binding character of the moral law associated with monotheism. He also draws attention to the personal esoteric beliefs and involvements of the Eranos scholars — excepting Scholem.
works.evidenceOffered: The Eranos lecture record, the three men's published work, and biographical material on their esoteric affiliations.
works.whoDisputes: The book was contested on publication; NO NAMED OPPONENT WAS VERIFIED THIS ROUND, which is a gap given how sharply contested it in fact was.
works.currentState: Live and consequential for this repo: it is the strongest published argument that the comparative-esotericism framing a survey site naturally reaches for is itself an ideological artefact of a particular mid-century circle.
works.siteRelevance: HIGH and uncomfortable. This site is a comparative survey of esoteric systems; Wasserstrom's argument is precisely about what goes wrong in that genre.

works.title: Kālī's Child: The Mystical and the Erotic in the Life and Teachings of Ramakrishna
works.author: Jeffrey J. Kripal (Rice University); doctoral supervisor Wendy Doniger
works.culture: American academic history of religions; psychoanalytic method

editions.publisher: University of Chicago Press
University of Chicago Press, second edition — incorporating corrections Kripal describes as minor errors identified by Swami Atmajnanananda

works.whatIsCriticised: THIS ROW IS THE OBJECT OF THE DISPUTE. Kripal argues that Ramakrishna's mystical experiences were profoundly erotic, reading them through a Freudian frame as bound up with homoerotic and paedophilic energies and with childhood trauma, and further argues that the Ramakrishna Order systematically suppressed and softened the biographical record. The evidentiary core is the guhya kathā — the 'secret talk' passages of Mahendranath Gupta's Bengali Kathāmṛta.
works.evidenceOffered: Bengali source work on the Kathāmṛta plus a psychoanalytic reading; the book won the American Academy of Religion's History of Religions Prize for Best First Book of 1995.
works.whoDisputes: THE LARGEST CRITICISM DOSSIER IN THIS SLICE, and it separates into four distinct kinds of objection which must not be collapsed. (1) TRANSLATION: named scholars dispute specific renderings — Jean Openshaw (1995), Swami Atmajnanananda (International Journal of Hindu Studies, August 1997), Rajat Kanta Ray (1997), Swami Tyagananda (2000). Disputed terms recorded in the reception literature include vyākulatā ('anxiety', rendered as erotic torment — J. S. Hawley disputing), uddīpana ('enkindling', rendered as homoerotic excitement), mānuṣ ('human being', rendered gender-specifically), tribhaṅga (a standard Krishna iconographic pose, rendered as 'cocked hips'), hṛt-padma ('lotus of the heart'), ramaṇ karo ('unite') and milan ('meeting'). (2) FACTUAL/DOCUMENTARY: Tyagananda documents age misidentifications — a fifty-year-old described as a boy, men in their thirties and forties as boy disciples — and argues the guhya kathā means esoteric scriptural meaning rather than shameful secret; he also notes the final Kathāmṛta volume was public from 1932, undercutting the suppression thesis. On Rāmchandra Datta's Jīvanvṛttānta, which Kripal called a suppressed scandalous biography, Vrajaprana and Atmajnanananda note nine Bengali editions existed by 1995 and Kripal acknowledged overplaying the suppression claim. (3) METHODOLOGICAL: Gerald Larson's 1998 exchange with Kripal charges reductionism; Alan Roland argues Freudian frames do not transfer to Asian cultures; Somnath Bhattacharyya and Larson note that neither Kripal nor Doniger has formal psychoanalytic training. (4) POLEMICAL/COMMUNITY: Narasingha Sil — himself the author of a psychoanalytic study of Ramakrishna and thanked in Kripal's preface — published a review in The Statesman (Calcutta, January 1997) ending in an obscenity and charging wilful distortion and manipulation of sources and inability to converse in Bengali; the paper closed the resulting correspondence after thirty-eight letters, reportedly without precedent, and declined William Radice's attempts to publish a defence. Huston Smith wrote in the Harvard Divinity School Bulletin (2001) that few books had offended Hindu sensibilities so grossly and called the work colonialism updated. Rajiv Malhotra's essay 'RISA LILA—I: Wendy's Child Syndrome' argued the Freudian apparatus is discredited.
works.defenders: Malcolm McLean's review in the Journal of the American Oriental Society (1997) called the treatment thorough, well documented and convincing. Brian Hatcher's 1999 survey of the reviews found the overall balance positive and at times highly laudatory. Kripal himself published a second edition, a response to Larson (1998), a response to Tyagananda, and 'The Tantric Truth of the Matter: A Forthright Response to Rajiv Malhotra', before announcing in late 2002 that after eight years, eight published essays, a second monograph and thousands of letters he was ending formal responses.
works.currentState: UNRESOLVED, and this file does not resolve it. Two efforts to have the book censored in India — 1996 and 2001 — failed in Parliament. J. S. Hawley moved from an early positive assessment (1998) toward a critical one by 2004. Hugh Urban, elsewhere a defender of psychoanalytically informed work, criticised the book's depiction of tantra as scandalous, seedy, sexy and dangerous. No scholarly consensus has emerged; the translation objections and the psychoanalytic objections have never been jointly adjudicated by a neutral body, and no such body exists.

works.whatIsCriticised: A VANTAGE POINT, and then a legality. Doniger writes the history from the point of view of women, dogs, horses and outcastes rather than through the male Brahminical narrative. The criticism divides sharply into (a) scholarly complaints about accuracy and focus and (b) a political and legal campaign about religious offence, and conflating the two is the standard error in every popular account of this affair.

Bharat Gupt charged misunderstanding of mythology and a politically motivated, left-aligned analysis. The Hindu American Foundation protested the National Book Critics Circle nomination on grounds of inaccuracy and bias. FAVOURABLE: David Arnold (Times Literary Supplement), David Shulman (New York Review of Books), Pankaj Mishra (New York Times), Library Journal, The Hindu. LEGAL: Dinanath Batra, founder of the Shiksha Bachao Andolan Samiti (affiliated to the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh), sued in 2011 under section 295A of the Indian Penal Code — deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings — with the matter coming to a head in February 2014.

The plaintiffs' counsel Monika Arora maintains she sought only correction of errors and characterises the republication as a way of avoiding a court test of those errors. Republication is a fact; vindication is not, and this file does not claim it.

works.title: 'Insufficient evidence to conclude whether or not Transcendental Meditation decreases blood pressure'
works.author: P. H. Canter & E. Ernst
works.culture: UK complementary-medicine evidence appraisal (Exeter)

editions.publisher: Journal of Hypertension 22.11; DARE structured abstract NBK70827

works.whatIsCriticised: A SPECIFIC HEALTH CLAIM AND THE INDEPENDENCE OF THE RESEARCHERS MAKING IT. Two findings, and the second is the one that matters for this slice: (a) the randomised-trial evidence is insufficient to conclude whether Transcendental Meditation lowers blood pressure; and (b) future research should be carried out by fully independent researchers not affiliated with the TM movement.
works.evidenceOffered: Systematic review of randomised clinical trials, with quality findings at the level of individual studies: procedures for establishing baseline blood pressure were adequate in only one trial; only one trial included a follow-on assessment; only one evaluable trial tested the effect in hypertensive individuals.

A 2014 Cochrane review of TM for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease (Hartley et al., CD010359.pub2) is the standing independent assessment. H. Schneider published a reply in the same journal arguing the ratings should be upgraded. General methodological criticism of the field persists — notably the reliance on waitlist and no-treatment comparators rather than active controls, which inflates apparent benefit through expectation, attention and group support.
